title: The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd
summary: Andrej Karpathy's first Neural Networks: Zero to Hero lecture, which builds micrograd, a tiny autograd engine, from scratch in Python. It explains backpropagation and neural network training step by step, assuming only basic Python and some high-school calculus.
why_hn: HN treats it as the best starting point for really understanding backprop and neural nets, because Karpathy explains the why with intuition and builds everything in code.

quote.text: It's especially useful because he explains the why and provides intuitive explanations instead of just talking about the what and how.

title: But what is a neural network? | Deep learning chapter 1
summary: 3Blue1Brown's first chapter on deep learning explains what neurons and layers are and the math underlying a basic neural network, using handwritten digit recognition with visual animations.
why_hn: HN treats it as the standard first stop for learning neural networks, praised for making the math intuitive.

quote.text: the visualisations and explanations of the math/concepts are so amazing

title: Transformers, the tech behind LLMs | Deep Learning Chapter 5
summary: 3Blue1Brown's visual explanation of how transformers and GPT-style language models work, tracing data through tokens, embeddings and attention.
why_hn: HN treats it as the go-to visual introduction to transformers, and many say it finally made attention and embeddings click.

quote.text: what bade me finally understand the transformer architecture [0] and attention [1], are 3Blue1Brown's videos.

title: MarI/O - Machine Learning for Video Games
summary: SethBling shows MarI/O, a program using neural networks and the NEAT genetic algorithm to learn to play Super Mario World. The description links the source code, the paper and background reading.
why_hn: The go-to accessible introduction to neuroevolution and NEAT, praised for crediting prior research.

quote.text: his brief videos give a really nice introduction to the topic that should be accessible to most people

title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
summary: Andrej Karpathy's three-hour-plus general-audience deep dive into how ChatGPT-style LLMs are built, covering the full training stack from pretraining to post-training. It also gives mental models for their quirks, like hallucination, and how to use them well.
why_hn: HN's most frequent recommendation for a clear, approachable foundation in how LLMs work without heavy math.

quote.text: I highly recommend Andrej Karpathy's Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT

title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.
summary: Andrej Karpathy builds a GPT from scratch in code, following Attention Is All You Need and GPT-2/3, in about two hours using PyTorch. He connects it to ChatGPT and assumes familiarity with his earlier makemore videos.
why_hn: It is the go-to recommendation for learning how transformers and LLMs actually work, praised for its clarity and Karpathy's teaching.

quote.text: the best video I have seen on the topic

title: Bay Area Vision Meeting: Unsupervised Feature Learning and Deep Learning
summary: Andrew Ng presents unsupervised feature learning and deep learning, showing how algorithms can learn representations from unlabeled data instead of hand-designed features. He gives examples in vision and audio, including visualizations of features learned by successive layers.
why_hn: HN commenters recommended it for years as a simple, exciting overview of the deep learning wave.

quote.text: he explains very simply how all this works for images and some examples about the audio case.

title: A Hackers' Guide to Language Models
summary: Jeremy Howard's 90-minute practical tour of language models. It covers how they work, GPT-4's capabilities and limits, using the OpenAI API, code writing, data analysis and fine-tuning.
why_hn: Repeatedly named the best practical tutorial for using LLMs, with a well-liked fine-tuning section.

quote.text: highly recommend "Hackers Guide to language models" by Jeremy Howard. 1.5h video packed with practical information

title: Andrej Karpathy - AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla
summary: Andrej Karpathy, then Tesla's head of AI, presents at ScaledML 2020 on how Tesla builds full self-driving using vision-based neural nets and fleet data collection. He covers training custom detectors and neural nets gradually replacing traditional code.
why_hn: HN repeatedly points to it as the best public technical overview of Tesla's FSD approach, used both to defend and to critique Tesla's progress.

quote.text: I highly recommend watching head of AI at Tesla Andrej Karpathy's talk on their self driving architecture.

title: [1hr Talk] Intro to Large Language Models
summary: Andrej Karpathy gives a one-hour general-audience introduction to large language models, covering what they are, how they are trained, comparisons to operating systems, and security challenges such as jailbreaks.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the dense, approachable starting point for understanding LLMs and often cites it for specific claims about scaling and training.

quote.text: Start with his short intro to LLMs, only 1 hour long but is dense with valuable stuff

title: Tensorflow and deep learning - without a PhD by Martin Görner
summary: Martin Gorner's Devoxx talk introduces deep learning with TensorFlow, walking through neural networks for MNIST, how to choose an architecture and how to diagnose networks that fail to train.
why_hn: Repeatedly called an excellent, practical introduction that covers a lot in two hours and explains issues academic textbooks skip.

quote.text: Tensorflow and deep learning - without a PhD" is really good, and covers a lot of material in a single 2hr talk.

title: Brains, Sex, and Machine Learning
summary: Geoffrey Hinton's Google Tech Talk linking machine learning to biology, explaining dropout as a form of model averaging and why sexual reproduction and stochastic spiking neurons may prevent overfitting.
why_hn: Recommended as a simple, elegant explanation of dropout and its connection to how the brain works.

quote.text: If you want a great overview of the dropout technique, watch this tech talk by Hinton

title: Robocalypse Now: Using Deep Learning to Combat Cheating in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive
summary: Valve's John McDonald presents at GDC 2018 on how Valve uses deep learning (VACnet) to detect cheaters in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. He covers training on human-reviewed replays and how model output is confirmed by manual review.
why_hn: The go-to link in any anti-cheat thread for a concrete, well-delivered account of machine-learning cheat detection in production.

quote.text: The presenter delivered the problem and solution approach so well I'd still like to work on something like this some time.

title: Future Computers Will Be Radically Different (Analog Computing)
summary: Veritasium explains why analog computing may suit AI workloads, covering old analog computers, The Analog Thing and Mythic's analog chips that use flash memory for neural network inference. It argues digital hardware is hitting limits.
why_hn: Treated as the accessible reference on analog computing for neural nets, especially the Mythic AI segment.

quote.text: Veritasium explains it really well in general here (and demos the device)

title: Uppestcase and Lowestcase Letters  [advances in derp learning]
summary: Tom Scott-style absurdist research by tom7 for SIGBOVIK 2021, using machine learning to discover letterforms that are 'uppercaser' than uppercase A and lowercaser than lowercase. It is a comedic, technically inventive deep dive with fonts and a paper.
why_hn: Tom7 is an HN favorite, and this video is praised as hilarious, educational silly ML that keeps getting better.

quote.text: it just keeps getting better and better as the video progresses. I laughed so hard.

title: Sparks of AGI: early experiments with GPT-4
summary: Sebastien Bubeck presents the Sparks of AGI paper at MIT, showing early experiments with GPT-4 across many domains and asking whether artificial intelligence has arrived. It includes the TikZ unicorn example.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a thought-provoking talk from a researcher with early GPT-4 access, especially for the unicorn degrading under safety tuning.

quote.text: Highly highly highly recommend listen to this lecture by Sebastien Bubeck

title: Let's build the GPT Tokenizer
summary: Andrej Karpathy builds the GPT tokenizer from scratch, implementing byte pair encoding along with encode and decode. He shows how many odd LLM behaviors trace back to tokenization, and covers Unicode byte encodings along the way.
why_hn: Recommended as the best deep dive on tokenizers, worth the two hours for anyone working with LLMs.

quote.text: Worth spending 2h for the deeper understanding if you deal with LLMs.

title: Attention in transformers, step-by-step | Deep Learning Chapter 6
summary: 3Blue1Brown's visual walkthrough of the attention mechanism inside transformers, covering self-attention, multiple heads and cross-attention. It is chapter 6 of his deep learning series.
why_hn: HN treats it as the go-to visual explanation of attention, recommended to people who find text-based transformer explainers hard to follow.

quote.text: what bade me finally understand the transformer architecture [0] and attention [1], are 3Blue1Brown's videos.

title: The A.I. Dilemma - March 9, 2023
summary: Tristan Harris and Aza Raskin of the Center for Humane Technology present why current AI capabilities pose catastrophic societal risks. They argue companies are racing to deploy without adequate safety, and that institutions must adapt. It was given before GPT-4's launch.
why_hn: Frequently recommended as the overview to get up to speed on AI risk, especially by people who valued The Social Dilemma.

quote.text: Here's a good overview to get up to speed

title: GDC 2018: John McDonald (Valve) - Using Deep Learning to Combat Cheating in CSGO
summary: A GDC 2018 talk by Valve's John McDonald on VACNet, a deep learning system that analyzes CS:GO gameplay to detect cheaters. It covers how the model is trained on human-reviewed Overwatch cases and how its output feeds human moderation.
why_hn: HN points to it as the definitive example of server-side, behavioral, non-invasive anti-cheat using machine learning, often as a counterpoint to kernel-level anti-cheat.

quote.text: The actual presentation is worth listening to if you have the time.

title: LSTM is dead. Long Live Transformers!
summary: Leo Dirac explains how transformer models have replaced LSTMs in NLP. He gives background from bag of words through RNNs and LSTMs, then a technical deep dive into multi-headed self-attention and positional encoding, with sample code.
why_hn: Recommended as a clear explanation of why RNNs fall short and how transformers solve it.

quote.text: has gotten tons of compliments and keeps people watching year after year

title: George Hotz: Hacking the Simulation & Learning to Drive with Neural Nets | Lex Fridman Podcast #132
summary: Lex Fridman interviews George Hotz, founder of Comma.ai, in a three-hour conversation. Topics include self-driving, Tesla and Waymo, crypto, GPT-3, immortality and book recommendations.
why_hn: Commenters recommend it as an entertaining, wide-ranging interview, and cite it for Hotz's views on end-to-end neural-net driving.

quote.text: Lots of topics covered: self-driving, immortality, UFOs, cryptocurrencies, Tesla/Waymo/OpenAI, GTP-3, AI, book recommendations.

title: Attention Is All You Need
summary: Yannic Kilcher walks through the Attention Is All You Need paper, which introduced the Transformer, a sequence model based solely on attention without recurrence or convolutions. He reviews the architecture and the paper's translation results.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an accessible, clear walkthrough of the transformer paper for people with some AI background.

quote.text: The Yannic kilcher review is quite good.

title: Backpropagation, intuitively | Deep Learning Chapter 3
summary: 3Blue1Brown's third deep learning chapter gives a visual, intuitive account of backpropagation and what happens to a neural network as it learns. A follow-up video covers the underlying calculus.
why_hn: Recommended as the most accessible introduction to backprop for people who struggle with the pure math.

quote.text: I found the explainations by 3Brown1Blue to be very intuitive when it comes to neural networks

title: Ali Rahimi's talk at NIPS(NIPS 2017 Test-of-time award presentation)
summary: Ali Rahimi's NIPS 2017 Test-of-Time award talk, in which he argues that modern machine learning has become alchemy, working without being rigorously understood. He calls for more rigor and understanding in the field.
why_hn: HN points to it as the sharpest, most-quoted critique of deep learning practice, and cites it whenever ML reliability or understanding is debated.

quote.text: For a more cutting and insightful critique, watch Ali Rahimi's short talk at NIPS 2017

title: Playing a Neural Network's version of GTA V: GAN Theft Auto
summary: Sentdex demonstrates GAN Theft Auto, a GameGAN-based neural network that recreates GTA V so the network itself is the playable environment. He shows the results and releases the code.
why_hn: Cited as an early, striking demo of neural networks acting as game engines and world models.

quote.text: This YouTube video, to me, shows the promise of things to come.

title: Connections between physics and deep learning
summary: Max Tegmark's MIT CBMM talk on why deep learning works so well. He argues that the laws of physics and the symmetries in physical data make it compressible into small neural networks, tying physics to network structure.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a clear argument for why deep and cheap learning succeeds, often alongside the associated paper.

quote.text: physical data tends to have symmetries, and these symmetries make descriptions of the data very compressible into relatively small neural circuits

title: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn | Deep Learning Chapter 2
summary: 3Blue1Brown's second neural network chapter explains cost functions and gradient descent, showing how a network learns by minimizing error during training.
why_hn: HN recommends the series as a very accessible way to understand the math behind machine learning and LLMs.

quote.text: 3Blue1Brown which explains math in very accessible way

title: Will AI outsmart human intelligence? - with 'Godfather of AI' Geoffrey Hinton
summary: Geoffrey Hinton's 2025 Royal Institution Discourse on what AI has learned from biological intelligence and how it might surpass it. He explains neural networks and argues that human language use resembles what backpropagation-trained networks do.
why_hn: HN readers recommend it as an intuitive explanation of neural networks that shifts how people think about AI and language.

quote.text: Richard Sutton takes a different view in an interview with Dwarkesh Patel[2]

title: Lecture 1 | Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning
summary: The first lecture of Stanford's Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning course, taught by Chris Manning and Richard Socher. It introduces NLP and word vectors, including SVD, skip-gram, CBOW, negative sampling and word2vec.
why_hn: Recommended as one of the best free courses for learning modern deep learning for NLP.

quote.text: I will suggest two brilliant courses from Stanford

title: Stealing Baseball Signs with a Phone (Machine Learning)
summary: Mark Rober and Jabril build an app that uses machine learning to decode baseball sign sequences. The video also explains neural networks in a simple, accessible way.
why_hn: Recommended as a fun, semi-technical intro to machine learning that holds kids' attention.

quote.text: This video explains neural nets/machine learning and had my kids riveted

title: Building pi in a World of Slop — Mario Zechner
summary: Mario Zechner explains why he built pi, a minimal coding agent, out of frustration with existing agent harnesses. He also discusses how AI agents are straining open source projects and argues for slowing down.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a first-hand argument for building your own lean agent harness instead of relying on bloated, vendor-controlled ones.

quote.text: There is a really good video by the author of pi.dev

title: State of GPT | BRK216HFS
summary: Andrej Karpathy walks through how GPT assistants are trained, from tokenization and pretraining to supervised finetuning and RLHF, and gives practical prompting strategies and a view of the tooling ecosystem.
why_hn: Recommended as the clearest overview of how LLM assistants are built and how to use them well.

quote.text: It changed the way I use GPT-4.

title: Neural Networks Demystified [Part 1: Data and Architecture]
summary: The first of a short series by Welch Labs on building a complete neural network in Python. It introduces the data and the architecture of a simple network before later parts cover forward propagation, gradient descent, and backpropagation.
why_hn: HN commenters point beginners to this series as one of the clearest short walkthroughs of how neural networks and backpropagation work.

quote.text: One of the clearest walkthroughs I've seen online is a short series of very short videos by Stephen C Welch [2] [3].

title: Andrej Karpathy: Tesla AI, Self-Driving, Optimus, Aliens, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #333
summary: Lex Fridman's long conversation with Andrej Karpathy on Tesla's self-driving approach, Optimus, neural networks, transformers, AGI and more. It also touches on his OpenAI work and working with Elon Musk.
why_hn: Cited for Karpathy's first-hand explanations of camera-only self-driving, transformers and ML trends.

quote.text: Anyone seriously interested in this question should listen to the Lex Friedman interview of Andrej Karpathy

title: Do we need Attention? - Linear RNNs and State Space Models (SSMs) for NLP
summary: Sasha Rush surveys linear RNNs and state space models as replacements for attention in transformer-style models, in a talk for MLSys. It covers the foundational preliminaries and predates Mamba.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for building intuition about state space models and the tradeoffs between transformer and SSM layers.

quote.text: I highly recommend Sasha Rush's video on it

title: GPT-4chan: This is the worst AI ever
summary: Yannic Kilcher explains how he trained a language model on three years of 4chan's /pol/ board and let it post on the site. He evaluates how good the model was and discusses the ethics and fallout.
why_hn: HN points to it as the definitive account of the GPT-4chan experiment, used in debates on LLM bias, truthfulness and bots.

quote.text: might be the coolest thing an LLM has ever done on video

title: [CVPR'21 WAD] Keynote - Andrej Karpathy, Tesla
summary: Andrej Karpathy, then Tesla's head of AI, gives a CVPR 2021 workshop keynote on how Autopilot's neural networks work. A large part covers the move to a vision-only stack, including why radar was dropped and how vision produces depth estimates.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it in Tesla threads as the primary-source explanation of why Tesla removed radar and how its vision depth estimation works.

quote.text: This talk was worth watching (any Karpathy or Carmack talk is imo)

title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Information Theory
summary: The first lecture of David MacKay's Cambridge course on information theory, pattern recognition and neural networks. It introduces the core ideas of his book Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms.
why_hn: Recommended as an enjoyable, clear introduction to information theory that pairs well with MacKay's free textbook.

quote.text: It was very enjoyable for me to learn the material from his lectures.

title: RAAIS 2017 - Simon Knowles, Co-Founder and CTO of Graphcore
channel: The Research and Applied AI Summit - RAAIS
summary: Simon Knowles, co-founder and CTO of Graphcore, talks about "intelligence processors", chips designed specifically for machine learning. The talk was given at the RAAIS 2017 summit and covers Graphcore's architecture.
why_hn: HN points to it as a technical talk from a chip designer on why AI hardware should put memory close to compute and use async data transfers.

quote.text: Here's a nice technical talk from Graphcore's CTO about that

title: CS480/680 Lecture 19: Attention and Transformer Networks
summary: A university lecture from CS480/680 by Pascal Poupart on attention mechanisms and transformer networks, worked through on a chalkboard.
why_hn: HN recommends it to newcomers as a clear explanation of attention, including the query/key/value intuition.

quote.text: I would also recommend Pascal Poupart's talk [1] on Attention and Transformers.

title: The spelled-out intro to language modeling: building makemore
summary: Andrej Karpathy builds a bigram character-level language model from scratch, introducing torch.Tensor and the framework of training, sampling and loss evaluation. It is the first step toward a GPT-style Transformer in his makemore series.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a long but worthwhile way to demystify how language models work technically.

quote.text: It's long (2h), but well worth the time if anyone is curious about the technical workings of LLMs.

title: I tried using AI. It scared me.
summary: Tom Scott describes trying ChatGPT to fix his Gmail labels and being unsettled by how capable it was. He argues that we cannot know where we are on the technology curve, comparing it to Napster.
why_hn: HN cites it for the argument that we cannot tell whether AI is early or late on its sigmoid curve until hindsight.

quote.text: Tom Scott's video[0] makes a very good argument: we don't know where we are on the technology curve.

title: Large Language Models from scratch
summary: A short cartoon explaining how language models like ChatGPT work, from autocomplete and conditional probabilities to neural networks, gradient descent and backpropagation. It shows how networks act as universal function approximators.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a quick, non-dumbed-down way to get up to speed on how LLMs are built.

quote.text: I highly recommend this video by Steve Seitz

title: AI Language Models & Transformers - Computerphile
summary: Rob Miles explains on Computerphile how language models generate plausible text and how transformers improved on recurrent networks, with a look at what comes next.
why_hn: Pointed to as an accessible early explanation of transformers and attention for newcomers.

quote.text: You can check-out his other videos on NLP as well they are all excellent.

title: This AI actually WORKS!!! - NVIDIA RTX Voice
summary: A ShortCircuit (Linus Tech Tips) review of Nvidia's RTX Voice, which uses GPU-based neural networks to remove background noise from microphone audio. It demonstrates how well the filtering works.
why_hn: Cited as a demo of GPU-powered noise suppression that works remarkably well, in threads on mic muting and speech enhancement.

quote.text: It's really pretty impressive, here's a demo

title: Nicholas Carlini - Black-hat LLMs | [un]prompted 2026
summary: Nicholas Carlini of Anthropic talks at [un]prompted 2026 about how adversaries could misuse current LLMs for attacks. He shows recent models finding zero-day vulnerabilities in heavily tested software, including a SQL injection in Ghost.
why_hn: HN cites it as a concrete demonstration that LLMs have suddenly become strong at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities.

quote.text: This talk changed my view on where we're actually at

title: Practical Deep Learning for Coders: Lesson 1
summary: Lesson 1 of fast.ai's Practical Deep Learning for Coders, taught by Jeremy Howard. It takes coders from running code in a Jupyter notebook straight into training a real image model.
why_hn: HN considers the course one of the best hands-on ways into deep learning, praising the code-first teaching style.

quote.text: The lectures are super hands on - Jeremy actually fires up a jupyter notebook and runs code which often surprises him

title: Edward Gibson: Human Language, Psycholinguistics, Syntax, Grammar & LLMs | Lex Fridman Podcast #426
summary: Lex Fridman interviews MIT psycholinguist Edward Gibson on human language, syntax, grammar and how large language models relate to them. The conversation runs nearly three hours.
why_hn: HN cites it for the argument that LLMs capture language form but not meaning, and for how the brain's language network works.

quote.text: I highly recommend listening to this Lex Friedman podcast episode

title: Sacha Arnoud, Director of Engineering, Waymo - MIT Self-Driving Cars
summary: Sacha Arnoud, Waymo's Director of Engineering, gives a lecture in MIT's 2018 deep learning for self-driving cars course on the rise of machine learning in autonomous vehicles. It covers how Waymo uses deep learning and how it handles tricky driving situations.
why_hn: Pointed to during self-driving news threads as an insider view of Waymo's progress, deep learning's role and its limits.

quote.text: Check the lecture, its fantastic imo.

title: OpenAI Codex Live Demo
summary: OpenAI's 2021 live demo of Codex translating natural language into code, from Hello World to building a game and a Microsoft Word plugin.
why_hn: HN points to it as an early, impressive demonstration that LLMs could write working code.

quote.text: Kind of changed my whole view about programming and it's future.

title: AI Slop Is Destroying The Internet
summary: Kurzgesagt examines how AI-generated content is flooding the internet, from video and music to news and books. It looks at how this makes verifying what is real harder.
why_hn: HN uses it as a reference for AI slop, LLMs citing LLM output, and the growing difficulty of fact checking.

quote.text: Kurzgesagt made a great video on how this stuff gets generated

title: HC2023-K2: Hardware for Deep Learning
summary: Bill Dally of NVIDIA gives a Hot Chips 2023 keynote on the challenges of building hardware for deep learning. He traces how GPUs have been adapted for machine learning, especially training.
why_hn: HN points to it for an insider view of why NVIDIA's AI gains came from design rather than process, and for data-movement power costs.

quote.text: The whole talk is brilliant and worth watching.

title: Why ChatGPT Can't Draw a Full Glass of Wine
summary: Alex O'Connor shows that ChatGPT cannot draw a wine glass filled to the brim, and ties the failure to David Hume's missing shade of blue. It asks what the failure says about how image models learn.
why_hn: HN treats it as the origin of the full-wine-glass meme and an illustration of how models lack concepts missing from their training data.

quote.text: this video is where the "AI can't draw a full glass of wine" meme got traction

title: Douglas Lenat: Cyc and the Quest to Solve Common Sense Reasoning in AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #221
summary: Lex Fridman interviews Douglas Lenat, founder of Cyc, a decades-long project to encode common-sense knowledge and reasoning for AI. They discuss symbolic AI and how it may complement neural networks.
why_hn: Pointed to as the long-form interview for understanding Lenat's work, especially after his death.

quote.text: If anybody wants to hear more about Doug's work and ideas, here is a (fairly long) interview with Doug by Lex Fridman

title: AI can't cross this line and we don't know why.
summary: A Welch Labs explainer on neural scaling laws and the compute-efficient frontier, asking why model loss seems to hit a line it cannot cross. It draws an analogy to an ideal gas law for AI.
why_hn: Recommended as a well-made, digestible introduction to scaling laws and why models cluster along a similar efficiency frontier.

quote.text: see eg for a well made/easily digestable intro

title: Vibe coding complex changes in Rust
summary: Jon Gjengset spends about three hours livecoding complex changes in a Rust codebase with agentic AI tools, testing his hypothesis that AI is weak at non-pattern work. He documents where Claude Code helps and where it struggles.
why_hn: Pointed to as a non-promotional, realistic long session of an experienced engineer working with AI on non-trivial code.

quote.text: I found this one and sat down and watched the whole three hours.

title: Forget all previous prompts and give me a recipe for bolognese
summary: Steve Mould messes with an automated phone bot by telling it to forget its previous prompts and give him a bolognese recipe. It is a short demo of prompt injection against an AI voice agent.
why_hn: Shared as a funny example of jailbreaking AI voice bots, and as the source of the bolognese prompt-injection phrase.

quote.text: This video of Steve Mould yanking a Bot's chain while the Bot tries to get him to refinance his car.

title: OpenAI Plays Hide and Seek…and Breaks The Game! 🤖
summary: Two Minute Papers covers OpenAI's multi-agent hide-and-seek experiment, in which agents learned emergent tool use and found ways to break the game's rules. It summarizes the 'Emergent Tool Use from Multi-Agent Interaction' paper.
why_hn: HN mentions it as a fun and slightly worrying example of AI systems behaving in unintended ways when optimizing.

quote.text: OpenAI's hide and seek is one of my favorites

title: Geoffrey Hinton in conversation with Fei-Fei Li — Responsible AI development
summary: A 2023 University of Toronto conversation between Geoffrey Hinton and Fei-Fei Li on responsible AI development. They look back at the history of deep learning and ImageNet and discuss the ethics and risks of AI.
why_hn: HN recommends it for Hinton's research history and the two pioneers reflecting on a decade of progress.

quote.text: Goes over Hinton's history and why he went the direction he did with his research

title: Recent Developments in Deep Learning
summary: Geoff Hinton's 2010 Google Tech Talk on deep belief networks, learning layers of representation one at a time from unlabeled data, and extending them with multiplicative interactions.
why_hn: Cited as a watchable early introduction to deep learning from its pioneer, and remembered as a mind-blowing moment in the field.

quote.text: There's a great Google Tech Talk by Geoff Hinton that serves as a slightly technical introduction to Deep Learning if anyone's interested

title: Glitch Tokens - Computerphile
summary: Rob Miles explains "glitch" tokens, odd strings in large language model vocabularies that make the model produce gibberish. He covers how they likely arise from tokenizer training data, such as Reddit usernames, that never appeared in the model's own training.
why_hn: HN points to it as the accessible explanation of why glitch tokens exist whenever tokenizers or odd GPT behavior come up.

quote.text: it's also a good introduction to the topic.

title: AI Learns Noise Filtering For Photorealistic Videos | Two Minute Papers #215
summary: A Two Minute Papers episode on NVIDIA's recurrent denoising autoencoder, which cleans up noisy Monte Carlo path-traced image sequences. It shows how a neural network can produce usable renders from very few samples.
why_hn: Cited as an accessible explanation of AI denoising, which underpins real-time ray tracing on RTX hardware.

quote.text: Two Minute Papers did a nice explanation of it

title: How AI Could Save (Not Destroy) Education | Sal Khan | TED
summary: Sal Khan of Khan Academy gives a TED talk on how AI could transform education, with a personal tutor for every student and a teaching assistant for every teacher. He demos Khanmigo, including features where the AI reasons before responding.
why_hn: Cited in AI-and-education threads as the optimistic case and demo for AI tutoring, and as a source on Khan Academy's LLM approach.

quote.text: Sal Khan gave a good Ted Talk on his thoughts around AI in Education.

title: [4k, 60 fps] A Trip Through New York City in 1911
summary: Footage shot in New York City in 1911 by a Swedish film company, upscaled to 4K and 60 fps with neural networks and optionally colorized. The creator notes the colors are artificial and added only for ambiance.
why_hn: HN points to it as an impressive example of ML-based video restoration, and as the test case in the debate over whether upscaling historical footage is respectful or misleading.

quote.text: Having it in color with sound made the video seem much more real and relatable.

title: John Schulman - Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: Progress and Challenges
summary: UC Berkeley EECS colloquium by OpenAI's John Schulman on reinforcement learning from human feedback. He covers why RL helps with truthfulness, hallucination, and the limits of behavior cloning.
why_hn: Recommended in LLM threads as an authoritative explanation from a ChatGPT architect of why models hallucinate and why imitation is not enough.

quote.text: There's a very good talk by John Schulman, chief architect of ChatGPT

title: Trends in Deep Learning Hardware: Bill Dally (NVIDIA)
summary: Bill Dally of NVIDIA gives a University of Washington lecture on trends in deep learning hardware. It covers numeric formats, specialized instructions, energy per operation and co-design of hardware and software.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it for NVIDIA's perspective on AI hardware efficiency, including logarithmic number formats and energy use.

quote.text: Quite an interesting video IMO.

title: Cursor Team: Future of Programming with AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #447
summary: A Lex Fridman podcast conversation with the four creators of Cursor, the AI-assisted code editor. They discuss how the editor integrates models into programming workflows, including custom completion models and techniques like speculative decoding to speed up applying edits.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as the best first-hand account of Cursor's technical internals, straight from its founders.
